---
title: "What EEG measures"
---

Before opening a recording, it helps to know what the numbers in it
are. This page has no code. It covers where the EEG signal comes from,
what it is good for, and what it cannot tell you. Those limits explain
many of the choices in the chapters that follow.

## Where the signal comes from

The first recording of electrical activity from the human scalp was
published almost a century ago [@berger1929]. The principle has not
changed: put electrodes on the head, and measure the tiny voltages
between them.

Those voltages come from neurons in the **cortex**, the folded outer
layer of the brain. When a neuron receives input from other neurons,
small electrical currents flow in and around it. The current from one
neuron is far too small to detect from outside the head. But the
cortex contains a great many **pyramidal cells** that are lined up side
by side, all pointing the same way, like the bristles of a brush. When
many thousands of them receive input at the same moment, their
currents add up to something large enough to reach the scalp
[@buzsaki2012; @luck2014].

Three things follow from that, and each one matters later.

**EEG reflects input, not output.** The signal comes mainly from the
slow currents produced when neurons *receive* input, not from the
brief spikes they fire to send signals on. Spikes are too short, and
too poorly lined up in time across neurons, to add up at the scalp
[@buzsaki2012].

**EEG only sees neurons acting together.** If a patch of cortex is busy
but its neurons are active at different moments, their currents cancel
and little reaches the scalp. A sizeable area of cortex has to be
active in step before anything is visible outside the head
[@cooper1965]. So EEG is a measure of *synchronised* activity. A flat
signal does not mean an idle brain.

**Direction matters.** Because the cells are lined up, the patch of
cortex behaves like a small battery with a positive and a negative
end. Whether an electrode above it sees a positive or a negative
voltage depends on which way the patch is facing, and the cortex is
folded, so patches face in every direction. This is why, in chapter 4,
the sign of a peak says nothing about "more" or "less" activity.

## From the cortex to the electrode

Between the cortex and the electrode lie fluid, the skull and the
scalp. The skull conducts electricity poorly, and the result is that
the signal from any one patch of cortex is **smeared** over a wide area
of the scalp by the time it gets out [@nunez2006]. Every electrode
picks up a blend of activity from many patches, and every patch
contributes to many electrodes.

This has two consequences you will meet again.

- **You cannot simply read off where activity is.** A peak at one
  electrode does not mean the activity is in the cortex directly
  beneath it. Working back from the scalp to the sources is possible
  only with extra assumptions, because many different arrangements of
  sources would give the same pattern on the scalp [@nunez2006]. In
  this tutorial we stay at the scalp and describe *where on the head*
  an effect is, not where in the brain.
- **Neighbouring electrodes look alike** for reasons that have nothing
  to do with brain areas talking to each other. They are partly
  recording the same sources. Chapter 7, on connectivity, is largely
  about dealing with this.

The signal is also small. By the time it reaches the scalp it is a few
tens of microvolts at most, smaller than the electrical signals from
blinking, from the muscles of the jaw and neck, and from the mains
wiring in the walls. That is why chapter 3 is devoted to cleaning.

## What EEG is good at, and what it is not

**It is fast.** Electrical signals travel from the cortex to the scalp
essentially instantly, and the amplifier measures them thousands of
times a second. EEG can separate events in the brain that are a few
thousandths of a second apart. Brain imaging with fMRI, by comparison,
measures changes in blood flow that unfold over seconds
[@logothetis2008]. If your question is *when* something happens, or in
what order, EEG is the right tool.

**It is poor at location.** Because of the smearing described above,
EEG cannot tell you precisely where in the brain a signal came from,
and it is nearly blind to structures deep in the brain, whose signals
are too weak by the time they reach the surface. If your question is
*where*, fMRI is far better.

**It is direct.** EEG measures the electrical activity of neurons
itself, not a slower side effect of it such as blood flow.

**It is cheap and harmless.** There is no radiation, no magnetic field
and no injection, and a participant can come back as often as needed.
The experiment used in this tutorial recorded the same people on five
separate visits, which would be hard to do any other way.

| | EEG | fMRI |
|---|---|---|
| measures | voltage from synchronised input to cortical neurons | blood oxygen, which follows neural activity |
| timing | thousandths of a second | seconds |
| location | poor; centimetres at best, and uncertain | good; millimetres |
| deep structures | mostly out of reach | visible |
| repeat visits | easy | expensive |

## What this means for the rest of the tutorial

- The signal is tiny and buried in larger signals from elsewhere, so
  we clean it (chapter 3) and average over many trials (chapter 4).
- Its strength is timing, so nearly every plot has time along the
  bottom, in fractions of a second.
- It reflects neurons acting in step, and much of that activity is
  rhythmic (chapter 5).
- Every electrode records a blend, so we are careful about what a
  pattern over the scalp can and cannot tell us (chapters 6 and 7).

Next, we open a recording.
